topics.name: Down syndrome
topics.kicker: Genetic condition from an extra chromosome 21 · Also called trisomy 21
topics.briefing: Down syndrome is a genetic condition that happens when a person has an extra copy of chromosome 21, which is why it is also called trisomy 21. It is named for John Langdon Down, an English doctor who described it in 1866, and in 1959 a French team including Jérôme Lejeune and Marthe Gautier found the extra chromosome. Every March 21, or 3/21, World Down Syndrome Day celebrates people with Down syndrome around the world.
topics.answerHtml: Down syndrome (accept Down’s syndrome or trisomy 21; prompt on trisomy; do not accept “Edwards syndrome” or “Patau syndrome”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Marthe Gautier [“goh-TYAY”] did much of the laboratory work behind a 1959 discovery about this condition, though most of the credit went to her colleague Jérôme Lejeune [“zhay-ROHM luh-ZHUHN”]. Their team in Paris found that children with this condition had 47 chromosomes instead of the usual 46.
tossups.r: It is named for an English doctor who described it in 1866. For 10 points, name this genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: In 2011, the United Nations General Assembly declared a yearly world awareness day for this condition, first observed by the U.N. in 2012. On that day, many people wear brightly colored or mismatched socks to celebrate people who have this condition.
tossups.r: That day falls on March 21, or 3/21, to stand for three copies of chromosome 21. For 10 points, name this genetic condition.

tossups.p: In 1866, an English doctor working at an institution in Surrey published a description of a group of his patients who shared several traits, and this condition was later named for him. Nearly a century later, in 1959, scientists in Paris discovered the genetic cause of this condition.
tossups.r: Its world awareness day is March 21. For 10 points, name this genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: Most cases of this condition begin with nondisjunction [“non-dis-JUNK-shun”], in which a pair of chromosomes fails to separate during meiosis while an egg or sperm cell forms. In a rarer mosaic form, the error usually happens after fertilization, so only some of a person’s cells are affected.
tossups.r: Its awareness day is March 21. For 10 points, name this genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: In a few percent of cases of this condition, extra genetic material is attached to another chromosome, often chromosome 14, in a change called a translocation. That form can sometimes be inherited from a parent whose chromosomes are rearranged but who does not have this condition.
tossups.r: It was described in 1866 by an English doctor. For 10 points, name this condition in which people have three copies of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: Because the gene for amyloid precursor protein lies on the chromosome involved in this condition, adults with this condition have a higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, often earlier in life than other people. Scientists also study mice bred with extra copies of many of the matching genes.
tossups.r: About half of babies born with this condition have a heart defect. For 10 points, name this genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: In 2000, the chromosome involved in this condition became the second human chromosome to have its DNA sequenced. A karyotype [“KAIR-ee-oh-type”], a picture of a person’s chromosomes lined up by size, can confirm this condition by showing three copies of that small chromosome.
tossups.r: Its world awareness day is held each March 21. For 10 points, name this genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: Actor Chris Burke, who has this condition, starred as Corky Thacher on the TV drama _Life Goes On_ from 1989 to 1993. Lauren Potter, an actress who also has this condition, played the cheerleader Becky Jackson on the TV series _Glee_.
tossups.r: Its world awareness day is March 21. For 10 points, name this genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: In 2020, Chris Nikic became the first person with this condition to finish an Ironman triathlon, completing a 2.4-mile swim, a 112-mile bike ride, and a 26.2-mile run in under 17 hours. Guinness World Records recognized his finish.
tossups.r: Its world awareness day is March 21. For 10 points, name this genetic condition in which people have three copies of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: Small white or gray spots on the iris called Brushfield spots are common in people with this condition. Other common traits include low muscle tone, eyes that slant upward, and a single crease across the palm, although every person with this condition is different.
tossups.r: It is named for an English doctor who described it in 1866. For 10 points, name this genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: In the United States, the average life expectancy of people with this condition rose from about 25 years in 1983 to about 60 years. The chance of having a baby with this condition rises with the mother’s age, but many babies with it are born to younger mothers, since younger women have more babies overall.
tossups.r: Its world awareness day is March 21. For 10 points, name this genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: Doctors describe three types of this condition: a standard type that makes up about 95 percent of cases, a translocation type, and a mosaic type in which only some of a person’s cells carry the extra genetic material.
tossups.r: People with the standard type have 47 chromosomes instead of 46. For 10 points, name this condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: American groups write this condition’s name without an apostrophe and s, since the doctor it honors did not have the condition, while British writers often include them. It is the most common chromosomal condition diagnosed in the United States.
tossups.r: Most people with it have some degree of intellectual disability. For 10 points, name this condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: Zack Gottsagen, an actor with this condition, starred in the 2019 film _The Peanut Butter Falcon_ and helped present an award at the 2020 Academy Awards. In the United States, October is this condition’s awareness month.
tossups.r: It is named for an English doctor who described it in 1866. For 10 points, name this genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

tossups.p: In most cases of this condition, the extra chromosome comes from the egg rather than the sperm. Like Edwards syndrome and Patau syndrome, this condition is a trisomy, but it involves a smaller chromosome than either of those conditions do.
tossups.r: Its world awareness day is March 21. For 10 points, name this genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

trap.title: Which trisomy?
trap.body: Down syndrome is the best-known trisomy, but quiz bowl also asks about Edwards syndrome (an extra chromosome 18) and Patau syndrome (an extra chromosome 13), plus sex-chromosome conditions like Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome. Saying only “trisomy” earns a prompt. The British form, “Down’s syndrome,” is accepted.
trap.fix: Chromosome 21, March 21, an English doctor in 1866, or Jérôme Lejeune in 1959 means Down syndrome. Chromosome 18 means Edwards syndrome, chromosome 13 means Patau syndrome, a missing X chromosome in females means Turner syndrome, and an extra X in males (XXY) means Klinefelter syndrome.
trap.line: Real answer line: Down syndrome (accept Down’s syndrome or trisomy 21; prompt on trisomy)

topics.name: Trees
topics.kicker: Tall, long-lived woody plants · Their yearly rings record history
topics.briefing: Trees are tall, woody plants with a single main trunk, and some are among the biggest and oldest living things on Earth. A coast redwood called Hyperion is the tallest known; General Sherman, a giant sequoia, is the largest known single-stem tree by volume; and bristlecone pines can live nearly 5,000 years. Most trees add one ring of wood every year, so scientists can read the rings to learn a tree’s age and even past climates.
topics.answerHtml: Trees (accept tree; prompt on woody plants or plants; do not accept “shrubs,” “forests,” or a specific kind such as “redwoods”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1929, a charred beam labeled HH-39, found at Show Low, Arizona, let the astronomer A. E. Douglass connect two long records of yearly growth rings and date many ancient Pueblo ruins. Douglass had begun studying the rings of these plants while searching for evidence of sunspot cycles.
tossups.r: The science he founded is called dendrochronology. For 10 points, name these tall, woody plants whose rings can be counted to find their age.

tossups.p: In 1964, a graduate student studying glaciers in Nevada cut down a bristlecone pine known as Prometheus, and counting its rings showed that it was nearly 5,000 years old. In 1957, Edmund Schulman found that another Great Basin bristlecone pine, Methuselah, was more than 4,700 years old.
tossups.r: Most of them add one growth ring each year. For 10 points, name these woody plants, which also include oaks, maples, and redwoods.

tossups.p: In 2006, naturalists Chris Atkins and Michael Taylor found a coast redwood named Hyperion, which at more than 115 meters is the tallest known living one of these plants. Its exact location in California’s Redwood National Park is kept secret to protect it.
tossups.r: Their trunks are covered in bark. For 10 points, name these tall, woody plants, which include oaks, maples, and pines.

tossups.p: Named in 1879 for a Civil War general, a giant sequoia called General Sherman is the largest known living single-stem one of these plants by volume. It grows in California’s Sequoia National Park and is thought to be more than 2,000 years old.
tossups.r: Most of them grow one ring of wood each year. For 10 points, name these tall plants with woody trunks, such as oaks, pines, and redwoods.

tossups.p: Pando, a grove of about 47,000 quaking aspen stems in Utah, is considered a single living thing because all of its stems share one root system, making it one of the heaviest known organisms. Aspen leaves tremble in light breezes because their stalks are flat.
tossups.r: Deciduous ones drop their leaves each fall. For 10 points, name these tall woody plants, such as oaks and pines.

tossups.p: Wangari Maathai won the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize after founding Kenya’s Green Belt Movement, which has planted tens of millions of these plants since 1977. J. Sterling Morton of Nebraska created a holiday devoted to planting them, first held in 1872.
tossups.r: That holiday is Arbor Day. For 10 points, name these woody plants that include oaks and maples.

tossups.p: Joyce Kilmer’s 1913 poem about these plants begins, “I think that I shall never see / A poem lovely as” one of them. In a 1971 Dr. Seuss book, the Lorax “speaks for” the Truffula ones that the Once-ler chops down to make Thneeds.
tossups.r: Their outer covering is bark. For 10 points, name these tall woody plants, such as oaks and pines.

tossups.p: In Norse mythology, a giant ash named Yggdrasil [“IG-druh-sil”] links the Nine Worlds, while a dragon gnaws at its roots. The Buddha is said to have reached enlightenment while meditating beneath one of these plants, a sacred fig, at Bodh Gaya in India.
tossups.r: Most add a new ring of wood every year. For 10 points, name these tall plants with woody trunks, such as oaks, pines, and maples.

tossups.p: As autumn days shorten, many of these plants stop making chlorophyll, revealing yellow and orange carotenoids that were in their leaves all along, while red colors come from newly made anthocyanins [“an-thoh-SY-uh-ninz”]. A layer of cells at the base of each leaf stalk then lets the leaf drop.
tossups.r: Those that lose their leaves every fall are called deciduous. For 10 points, name these woody plants that include maples and oaks.

tossups.p: In these plants, a thin layer called the vascular cambium adds new xylem toward the inside and new phloem toward the outside, while older xylem at the center becomes darker heartwood that no longer carries water. A separate cork cambium makes the dead cork cells of the outer covering.
tossups.r: That outer covering is bark. For 10 points, name these woody plants whose trunks add a ring each year.

tossups.p: Balsa wood is classified as a hardwood, even though it is very soft, because it comes from a flowering example of these plants, while softwoods come from conifers. Palms can look like these plants but never make true wood, because they have no vascular cambium.
tossups.r: Oaks and maples are examples. For 10 points, name these tall plants that usually have one woody trunk.

tossups.p: A 2015 study led by Thomas Crowther estimated that Earth has about 3 trillion of these plants, roughly 400 for every person. Cutting a ring of bark all the way around one of them, called girdling, kills it by blocking the flow of sugar to its roots.
tossups.r: Most of them have a single trunk covered in bark. For 10 points, name these woody plants, such as oaks and pines.

tossups.p: Australia’s mountain ash, a kind of eucalyptus, is the tallest flowering one of these plants, while baobabs [“BAY-oh-babz”] store water inside their enormous, swollen trunks. Many mangroves, which grow in salty coastal water, send up “breathing” roots called pneumatophores [“noo-MAT-uh-forz”].
tossups.r: Their rings show their age. For 10 points, name these woody plants, which include oaks, maples, and pines.

tossups.p: Chestnut blight, a fungal disease first noticed at New York’s Bronx Zoo in 1904, nearly wiped out the American chestnut, one of these plants. Since it was found near Detroit in 2002, an Asian beetle called the emerald ash borer has killed millions of North American ashes.
tossups.r: Oaks and maples are other examples. For 10 points, name these woody plants that make up forests.

tossups.p: Suzanne Simard’s 1997 research suggested that these plants can share carbon through networks of fungi on their roots, nicknamed the “wood wide web.” The study of these plants is called dendrology, from a Greek root that also names the branching dendrites of neurons.
tossups.r: Oaks, pines, and maples are examples. For 10 points, name these tall plants with woody trunks.

trap.title: Name the group, not one
trap.body: Tossups about trees love famous individuals and kinds: Hyperion, General Sherman, Methuselah, redwoods, and bristlecone pines. If the question asks for “these plants” and mixes examples from many groups, naming one kind, like “redwoods” or “conifers,” is wrong. “Forests” and “wood” are different answers, and plain “plants” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “these plants” or “these woody plants,” with examples from different families (oaks, pines, palms, baobabs), means trees. Name a single kind only when the question says “this species,” “this genus,” or “these conifers.” Naked seeds and cones can point to the separate answer Gymnosperms.
trap.line: Real answer line: Trees (accept tree; prompt on woody plants; do not accept a specific kind of tree)

topics.name: Alveoli
topics.kicker: Tiny air sacs of the lungs · Where oxygen enters the blood
topics.dates: About 300 million in an adult’s lungs
topics.briefing: Alveoli are tiny, balloon-like air sacs at the ends of your smallest airways, clustered like bunches of grapes. An adult’s lungs hold roughly 300 million of them, and each is wrapped in capillaries, so oxygen can slip into the blood while carbon dioxide slips out. A soapy coating called surfactant keeps them from collapsing, and babies born very early, before their lungs make enough of it, can have trouble breathing.
topics.answerHtml: Alveoli (accept alveolus or alveolar sacs; prompt on air sacs; do not accept “bronchioles” or “lungs”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1959, Mary Ellen Avery and Jere Mead showed that premature babies with a serious breathing disorder lacked a substance that normally coats the inside of these structures. That soapy substance, surfactant, lowers surface tension so these structures do not collapse when a person breathes out.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange takes place.

tossups.p: In 1980, Tetsuro Fujiwara successfully treated premature babies by putting replacement surfactant into their lungs to keep these structures open. Babies born too early may not yet make enough surfactant, which can lead to respiratory distress syndrome, also called hyaline [“HY-uh-lin”] membrane disease.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs, wrapped in capillaries, where oxygen enters the blood.

tossups.p: The law of Laplace [“luh-PLAHSS”] explains why, without surfactant, smaller examples of these structures would collapse and empty into larger ones. Small openings called the pores of Kohn connect neighboring examples of these structures, so air can pass between them.
tossups.r: Their walls are only one cell thick. For 10 points, name these tiny sacs at the ends of the bronchioles where gas exchange happens.

tossups.p: Birds lack these structures; instead, air flows one way through tubes called parabronchi, which are lined with tiny air capillaries. In humans, the air left in the trachea and bronchi that never reaches these structures is called anatomical dead space.
tossups.r: These structures are grouped in clusters like bunches of grapes. For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs in the lungs.

tossups.p: Macrophages nicknamed “dust cells” crawl along the inner surfaces of these structures, swallowing dust and germs that get past the mucus in the airways. Coal dust that builds up in these structures over many years can scar the lungs, causing black lung disease.
tossups.r: Networks of capillaries surround them. For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood.

tossups.p: An inherited shortage of the protein alpha-1 antitrypsin [“an-tee-TRIP-sin”] lets enzymes break down the walls of these structures, causing emphysema earlier in life than usual. More often, emphysema is caused by smoking, which destroys these structures and leaves fewer, larger spaces with less surface area.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these air sacs of the lungs, which are wrapped in capillaries.

tossups.p: Thin, flat type I cells cover most of the inner surface of these structures, while rounder type II cells secrete surfactant and can divide to replace damaged type I cells. Elastic fibers in their walls help these structures spring back as a person breathes out.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tiny sacs in the lungs, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.

tossups.p: Oxygen’s partial pressure is about 100 millimeters of mercury inside these structures but only about 40 in the blood arriving from the body, so oxygen diffuses into the blood. At high altitude, lower air pressure leaves less oxygen inside these structures, so less oxygen crosses into the blood.
tossups.r: Each one is wrapped in capillaries. For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles.

tossups.p: These structures take their name from a Latin word for a “small cavity,” which is also used for the sockets that hold teeth in the jawbone. The bony ridge behind the upper front teeth, used to make sounds like t and d, is named with the same Latin word.
tossups.r: Each one is wrapped in capillaries. For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs in the lungs, where gas exchange occurs.

tossups.p: The barrier between the air inside these structures and the blood in the surrounding capillaries is only about half a micrometer thick. An adult’s lungs contain roughly 300 million of these structures, giving them a surface area for gas exchange dozens of times larger than the skin’s.
tossups.r: Oxygen diffuses from them into the blood. For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs at the ends of the smallest airways.

tossups.p: In pulmonary fibrosis, scar tissue thickens the walls of these structures, making it harder for oxygen to pass through them. In pneumonia, an infection makes these structures fill with fluid, so less oxygen can reach the blood.
tossups.r: They sit at the ends of the bronchioles. For 10 points, name these tiny sacs in the lungs where oxygen enters the blood.

tossups.p: In 1929, Kurt von Neergaard showed that lungs filled with liquid are easier to inflate than lungs filled with air, because surface tension inside these structures resists stretching. The phospholipid DPPC is the main ingredient of the substance that lowers that surface tension inside these structures.
tossups.r: That substance is surfactant. For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles.

tossups.p: A newborn baby has only a fraction of the adult number of these structures, which keep forming for years after birth. Before birth, these structures are filled with fluid instead of air, and a baby’s first breaths help clear that fluid.
tossups.r: Each is wrapped in capillaries. For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood.

tossups.p: After surgery, patients often use a device called an incentive spirometer to take slow, deep breaths that help keep these structures from collapsing, a problem called atelectasis [“at-uh-LEK-tuh-sis”]. Without enough surfactant, these structures also tend to collapse.
tossups.r: They are clustered at the ends of the bronchioles. For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs in the lungs, where gas exchange happens.

tossups.p: Oxygen leaving these structures crosses a thin respiratory membrane made of their wall, a shared basement membrane, and the wall of a capillary. Asthma narrows the bronchioles that lead to these structures, but unlike emphysema, it does not destroy these structures themselves.
tossups.r: Red blood cells pick up the oxygen that leaves them. For 10 points, name these tiny air sacs in the lungs.

trap.title: Sacs, not tubes
trap.body: Lung tossups move through a chain of answers: the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, and the capillaries around them, plus the lungs as a whole. Alveoli are the dead-end sacs where gas exchange happens; bronchioles are the tiny tubes that lead to them. Saying just “air sacs” earns a prompt, and birds have different “air sacs” that do not exchange gases at all.
trap.fix: “Surfactant,” “type I and type II cells,” “dust cells,” “300 million,” and “emphysema destroys their walls” mean alveoli. Smooth muscle that tightens during an asthma attack means bronchioles, vessels one cell thick mean capillaries, and “these paired organs” means the lungs.
trap.line: Real answer line: Alveoli (accept alveolus; prompt on air sacs; do not accept “bronchioles”)

topics.name: Active transport
topics.kicker: Moving substances against a concentration gradient · Usually powered by ATP
topics.briefing: Active transport is how a cell moves substances “uphill,” from where they are scarce to where they are already crowded. Because that goes against the natural spread of diffusion, it costs energy, usually ATP, and it is done by protein pumps in the cell membrane. A famous example is the sodium-potassium pump, which pushes three sodium ions out of a cell and brings two potassium ions in for each ATP it uses.
topics.answerHtml: Active transport (accept primary or secondary active transport; prompt on cotransport or pumping; do not accept “passive transport,” “diffusion,” or “osmosis”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Jens Christian Skou discovered an enzyme in crab nerve cells in 1957 that carries out this process, and he shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for that discovery. Heart drugs such as digoxin, which comes from foxglove plants, block that enzyme, and so does the poison ouabain [“WAH-bayn”].
tossups.r: That enzyme, the sodium-potassium pump, moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. For 10 points, name this process that moves substances against their concentration gradient using energy.

tossups.p: Salt-loving archaea use a light-powered protein called bacteriorhodopsin [“bak-teer-ee-oh-roh-DOP-sin”] to carry out this process, pushing hydrogen ions out of the cell. In mitochondria, protein complexes use energy taken from electrons to perform this process on hydrogen ions, building up a gradient.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that uses energy to move substances from low to high concentration, unlike diffusion.

tossups.p: Oral rehydration solution, a mix of salt and sugar in clean water, has saved many lives during cholera outbreaks because intestinal cells pull in sodium and glucose together, and water follows. That pairing relies on a sodium-glucose symporter called SGLT1, which uses the secondary form of this process.
tossups.r: Pumps powered by ATP also carry it out. For 10 points, name this process that uses energy to move substances against their concentration gradient.

tossups.p: V-type pumps perform this process on hydrogen ions to keep lysosomes and plant vacuoles acidic. Cells in the stomach lining also perform it, pumping hydrogen ions into the stomach in exchange for potassium ions to make stomach acid, and drugs called proton pump inhibitors block those pumps.
tossups.r: The sodium-potassium pump is a famous example. For 10 points, name this energy-using process that moves substances against their concentration gradient.

tossups.p: Thyroid cells use a sodium-iodide symporter to perform the secondary form of this process, gathering iodide until it is far more concentrated inside them than in the blood. That symporter is powered by a sodium gradient that another protein builds using ATP.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which cells use energy to move substances against their concentration gradient.

tossups.p: Companion cells in a plant’s phloem use proton pumps to build up a gradient of hydrogen ions, which then helps them pull in sucrose by the secondary form of this process. Root hair cells, which are packed with mitochondria, use this process to absorb mineral ions like nitrate from the soil.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which cells spend energy, usually from ATP, to move substances against their concentration gradient.

tossups.p: In the antiport kind of this process, two substances cross a membrane in opposite directions, as when heart muscle cells push calcium out while letting sodium in through a sodium-calcium exchanger. In the symport kind, two substances cross in the same direction.
tossups.r: Both kinds are forms of cotransport. For 10 points, name this process that moves molecules against their concentration gradient using energy.

tossups.p: Calcium pumps that perform this process in muscle cells are P-type pumps, which change shape after ATP attaches a phosphate group to them. After a muscle contracts, those pumps pull calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum [“sar-koh-PLAZ-mik reh-TIK-yoo-lum”] so the muscle can relax.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, also carried out by the sodium-potassium pump, that uses energy to move substances against a concentration gradient.

tossups.p: The main pump that carries out this process in animal cells is called electrogenic, because each cycle moves one more positive charge out of the cell than in. That pump helps keep the inside of a resting neuron at about −70 millivolts compared with the outside.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, performed by the sodium-potassium pump, that moves substances against their concentration gradient.

tossups.p: _E. coli_ bacteria bring lactose inside with lactose permease, which carries each sugar molecule in along with a hydrogen ion in a form of this process. That permease is made from a gene in the lac operon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that uses energy to move substances against their concentration gradient, unlike diffusion.

tossups.p: Some cancer cells resist chemotherapy by making P-glycoprotein, a pump powered by ATP that performs this process to push drugs back out of the cell. P-glycoprotein belongs to a large family of pumps named for the ATP-binding cassette, or ABC, part of their structure.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that uses energy to move substances across a membrane against their concentration gradient.

tossups.p: Diabetes drugs called SGLT2 inhibitors block a kidney protein that performs this process, letting extra sugar leave the body in urine. Normally, cells lining the kidney’s proximal tubules use this process to reclaim nearly all of the glucose from the filtered fluid.
tossups.r: Protein pumps carry it out. For 10 points, name this process that moves substances from lower to higher concentration using energy.

tossups.p: Thermodynamically, this process is endergonic, or “uphill,” so cells must couple it to an energy-releasing reaction such as the breakdown of ATP. Facilitated diffusion uses similar carrier proteins, but it can only move substances down their concentration gradients, without spending energy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, carried out by pumps, that moves substances against their concentration gradient.

tossups.p: Saltwater fish use special “chloride cells” in their gills to pump extra salt out of their bodies, while freshwater fish use similar cells to pull in salt from the dilute water around them. Both jobs rely on this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that moves ions against their concentration gradient using energy, usually from ATP.

tossups.p: In the primary form of this process, a pump uses ATP directly, while in the secondary form, a substance flowing down its gradient, usually sodium or hydrogen ions, provides the energy to move another substance up its gradient.
tossups.r: Root hair cells use it to take up minerals. For 10 points, name this process that moves molecules against their concentration gradient, unlike diffusion and osmosis.

trap.title: Active or passive?
trap.body: Diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and osmosis are passive: substances move down their concentration gradient, and the cell spends no energy. Active transport is the opposite, using energy, usually ATP, to push substances up their gradient. Facilitated diffusion is the sneaky one, because it also uses membrane proteins, but it never moves anything against the gradient.
trap.fix: “Against the gradient,” “uphill,” “pump,” “ATP,” “sodium-potassium pump,” or “cotransport” means active transport. “Down the gradient,” “no energy,” or “channel proteins” means diffusion or facilitated diffusion, and water crossing a membrane means osmosis. Endocytosis and exocytosis, which wrap material in vesicles, are separate answers.
trap.line: Real answer line: Active transport (accept primary or secondary active transport; prompt on cotransport; do not accept “passive transport” or “diffusion”)

topics.name: Bacteriophages
topics.kicker: Viruses that infect bacteria · Their name means “bacteria eaters”
topics.briefing: Bacteriophages, or phages, are viruses that attack only bacteria. Many look like tiny lunar landers: a many-sided head full of DNA sits on a hollow tail with spidery legs that grab a bacterium so the virus can inject its genes. Frederick Twort and Félix d’Hérelle discovered them in 1915 and 1917, and doctors are testing them again as a weapon against germs that antibiotics can no longer kill.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a 1925 novel by Sinclair Lewis, the scientist Martin Arrowsmith discovers a germ-killing agent he calls the “X Principle,” but Félix d’Hérelle [“day-REL”] has already described it as one of these viruses. Arrowsmith later tests the agent during an outbreak of plague on a Caribbean island.
tossups.r: Many of these viruses look like tiny lunar landers. For 10 points, name these viruses that attack bacteria, whose name means “bacteria eaters.”

tossups.p: In 1896, Ernest Hanbury Hankin reported that water from India’s Ganges and Yamuna rivers could kill the bacteria that cause cholera, an effect that may have come from these viruses. In 1915, Frederick Twort described a “glassy,” see-through change in colonies of bacteria that was caused by these viruses.
tossups.r: Félix d’Hérelle named them two years later. For 10 points, name these viruses that infect bacteria, such as T4 and lambda.

tossups.p: In 1952, two scientists used a kitchen blender to shake the empty protein coats of the T2 type of these viruses off of E. coli cells. Radioactive phosphorus marking the viruses’ DNA had gone into the cells, but radioactive sulfur marking their protein had not.
tossups.r: That Hershey–Chase experiment showed that DNA is the genetic material. For 10 points, name these viruses that infect bacteria.

tossups.p: Salvador Luria and Max Delbrück’s 1943 “fluctuation test” showed that E. coli cells become resistant to these viruses through random mutations that happen before the viruses ever arrive. Luria and Delbrück shared the 1969 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Alfred Hershey for their research on these viruses.
tossups.r: In the lytic cycle, these viruses multiply inside a host cell until it bursts. For 10 points, name these viruses that infect bacteria.

tossups.p: Esther Lederberg discovered lambda, one of these viruses, hiding in a lab strain of E. coli. In the lysogenic cycle, the DNA of these viruses hides inside the host’s chromosome and is copied every time the host cell divides.
tossups.r: In the lytic cycle, they instead make many copies and burst the cell. For 10 points, name these viruses that infect bacteria.

tossups.p: In 1961, Francis Crick and Sydney Brenner added and removed single DNA bases in a gene of the T4 type of these viruses and showed that the genetic code is read three bases at a time. Seymour Benzer had already mapped that same gene region, called rII [“R-two”], in great detail.
tossups.r: These viruses inject their DNA into host cells such as E. coli. For 10 points, name these viruses, such as T4 and lambda, that infect bacteria.

tossups.p: In 1977, Frederick Sanger’s team read every DNA base of Phi X 174, one of these viruses, making it the first DNA genome ever sequenced. A year earlier, Walter Fiers’s lab had sequenced the complete genome of MS2, a member of this group that carries RNA instead of DNA.
tossups.r: Many of these viruses have a many-sided head, a tail, and tail fibers. For 10 points, name these viruses that infect bacteria.

tossups.p: George Smith and Gregory Winter shared part of the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for a technique that makes these viruses carry a chosen protein on their outer coat. Winter used that technique to build new antibody medicines.
tossups.r: These viruses can reproduce only inside bacteria. For 10 points, name these viruses, whose name means “bacteria eaters.”

tossups.p: The spacers stored in a bacterium’s CRISPR regions are short copies of DNA from past attacks by these viruses, which help Cas enzymes find and cut the same invaders again. Restriction enzymes, which chop up foreign DNA, were discovered because they block these viruses from growing in some bacteria.
tossups.r: Their hollow tails inject DNA into their hosts. For 10 points, name these viruses that infect bacteria, such as T4 and lambda.

tossups.p: In 2016, doctors at the University of California, San Diego, treated Tom Patterson’s infection, which no antibiotic could stop, by giving him these viruses. In 1923, George Eliava founded an institute in Tbilisi, Georgia, that kept using these viruses as medicine after antibiotics took over in the West.
tossups.r: Félix d’Hérelle pioneered using them as medicine. For 10 points, name these viruses that kill bacteria.

tossups.p: When these viruses are spread over a dish covered with a thin “lawn” of bacteria, they leave behind clear, round spots called plaques where the cells have been killed. Scientists count those plaques to measure how many of these viruses a sample holds.
tossups.r: Félix d’Hérelle named these viruses in 1917. For 10 points, name these viruses whose name means “bacteria eaters.”

tossups.p: The genes for the toxins made by the bacteria that cause diphtheria and cholera are carried by some of these viruses, so a harmless strain can turn dangerous after one of them hides its DNA inside the bacterium. That change is called lysogenic conversion.
tossups.r: These viruses inject their DNA through a hollow tail. For 10 points, name these viruses that infect bacteria.

tossups.p: André Lwoff showed that ultraviolet light could wake up the hidden DNA of these viruses inside bacteria, work that helped earn him a share of the 1965 Nobel Prize. In 1952, Norton Zinder and Joshua Lederberg found that these viruses can carry genes from one Salmonella cell to another, a process called transduction.
tossups.r: These viruses usually keep their DNA in a many-sided head. For 10 points, name these viruses, such as T4 and lambda, that infect bacteria.

tossups.p: Scientists estimate that about 10 to the 31st power of these viruses exist on Earth, making them the most numerous biological entities on the planet. In the oceans, they kill huge numbers of bacteria every day, releasing nutrients back into the water.
tossups.r: Each kind usually attacks just one species of bacteria. For 10 points, name these viruses, whose name means “bacteria eaters.”

tossups.p: The T4 type of these viruses lands on a host cell using six long tail fibers, then contracts its tail like a syringe to inject its DNA through the cell wall. A many-sided protein head called a capsid holds that DNA.
tossups.r: Their shape is often compared to a lunar lander. For 10 points, name these viruses that infect bacteria.

trap.title: Virus, not bacterium
trap.body: Bacteriophages are viruses, so answering just “virus” is on the right track but only earns a prompt. Their hosts are bacteria such as E. coli, and naming the host is wrong. Macrophages and phagocytes are traps too: those are white blood cells that swallow germs, and their names share the same Greek root for “eat.”
trap.fix: If the question says “these viruses” and mentions tails, T4, lambda, the lytic or lysogenic cycle, plaques, or Hershey and Chase, say “bacteriophages” or just “phages.” Save “viruses” for questions about the whole group, which also includes the causes of the flu and measles.
trap.line: Real answer line: Bacteriophages (accept phages; prompt on viruses; do not accept “bacteria”)

topics.name: Glycine
topics.kicker: Simplest amino acid · Its side chain is a single hydrogen atom
topics.briefing: Glycine is the simplest of the 20 amino acids that build your proteins: where the others carry bigger side chains, glycine has just a single hydrogen atom. Its name comes from the Greek word for “sweet,” because it tastes sugary. Every third building block in collagen is glycine, it helps quiet nerve signals in your spinal cord, and NASA scientists even found it in dust brought back from a comet.
topics.answerHtml: Glycine (accept Gly or aminoacetic acid; prompt on amino acid; do not accept other amino acids)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1820, the French chemist Henri Braconnot [“bra-kaw-NOH”] boiled gelatin with sulfuric acid and isolated sweet-tasting crystals that he called “sugar of gelatin.” Those crystals were this compound, whose name comes from the Greek word for “sweet.”
tossups.r: Its side chain is just one hydrogen atom, making it the simplest of the 20 standard amino acids. For 10 points, name this amino acid.

tossups.p: The poison strychnine [“STRIK-nyne”] causes severe muscle spasms by blocking this compound’s receptors, which are chloride channels on nerve cells in the spinal cord and brainstem. Along with GABA, this compound is one of the body’s main inhibitory neurotransmitters.
tossups.r: It is the only standard amino acid that is not chiral. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid, whose side chain is a hydrogen atom.

tossups.p: In 2009, NASA scientists reported finding this compound in dust from Comet Wild 2 [“VILT two”] that the Stardust spacecraft had carried back to Earth. It was also found in the Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia in 1969.
tossups.r: In collagen, every third amino acid is this one. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid, whose side chain is just a hydrogen atom.

tossups.p: The most common three-unit pattern in collagen’s chains is this amino acid followed by proline and hydroxyproline. This amino acid is the only one small enough to fit in the crowded center of collagen’s triple helix, where the three chains wind together.
tossups.r: Gelatin is rich in it, since every third amino acid in collagen is this one. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid.

tossups.p: The body uses this amino acid as a starting material for heme, the iron-holding part of hemoglobin in red blood cells. Its carbon and nitrogen atoms are also built into the rings of the purine bases adenine and guanine.
tossups.r: It is the only standard amino acid that has no chiral carbon. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid.

tossups.p: Silk fibroin [“FY-broh-in”], the main protein in silkworm silk, is built mostly from repeating units of this amino acid and alanine, which pack into tightly stacked sheets. The proteins in spider silk are also rich in this amino acid.
tossups.r: Its one-letter code is G. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid, whose side chain is just a hydrogen atom.

tossups.p: In 1901, Emil Fischer and Ernest Fourneau [“foor-NOH”] made the first man-made dipeptide by linking two units of this amino acid with a peptide bond. The chemical formula of this amino acid is C2H5NO2.
tossups.r: Its side chain is just a hydrogen atom. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid, which also works as a neurotransmitter.

tossups.p: Replacing one of the two hydrogen atoms on this amino acid’s central carbon with a methyl group turns it into alanine, the next-simplest amino acid. In the spinal cord, this amino acid acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter, quieting the nerve cells that control muscles.
tossups.r: It has no L or D form because it is not chiral. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid.

tossups.p: This compound was one of the most plentiful amino acids made in Stanley Miller’s 1953 experiment, which sent electric sparks through methane, ammonia, hydrogen, and water vapor. Chemists describe it as acetic acid, the acid in vinegar, with an amino group in place of one hydrogen atom.
tossups.r: Its side chain is a single hydrogen atom. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid, which makes up about a third of collagen.

tossups.p: Because it has no bulky side chain to bump into its neighbors, this amino acid lets a protein’s backbone twist and bend more freely than any other amino acid does. That flexibility lets it sit in tight turns, and like proline, it tends to break up alpha helices.
tossups.r: Its central carbon holds two hydrogen atoms, so it is not chiral. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid.

tossups.p: In the liver, bile acids such as cholic acid are joined to either taurine or this amino acid to make the bile salts that help digest fats. In the kidneys, this amino acid and arginine are the starting materials for creatine, which muscles use to store energy.
tossups.r: Its name comes from the Greek word for “sweet.” For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid.

tossups.p: The antioxidant glutathione [“gloo-tuh-THY-ohn”] is a chain of three amino acids: glutamate, cysteine, and this one. Unlike the other 19 standard amino acids, this one has no mirror-image L and D forms, because it is not chiral.
tossups.r: In the spinal cord, it works as an inhibitory neurotransmitter. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid.

tossups.p: An enzyme that uses a form of folate turns the amino acid serine into this amino acid by removing one carbon atom. Because the body can make it this way, this amino acid is called nonessential, meaning it does not have to come from food.
tossups.r: In collagen, every third amino acid is this one. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid.

tossups.p: In the genetic code, the four codons GGU, GGC, GGA, and GGG all stand for this amino acid. Its receptors in the spinal cord and brainstem are chloride channels that make nerve cells less likely to fire.
tossups.r: It is the only standard amino acid that is not chiral. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid.

tossups.p: In 2016, scientists reported that the European probe Rosetta had detected this compound in the gas streaming off Comet 67P. Rosetta also found phosphorus there, another key ingredient for life.
tossups.r: This compound is also an inhibitory neurotransmitter. For 10 points, name this simplest amino acid, whose side chain is a single hydrogen atom.

Its name comes from the Greek word for “sweet,” and it tastes sweet
Its four codons all begin with GG (GGU, GGC, GGA, GGG), and its one-letter code is G
Its receptors are chloride channels, and the poison strychnine blocks them

Very flexible, so it is common in tight turns, and like proline it tends to break up alpha helices

In 2009, NASA reported finding it in comet dust that the Stardust spacecraft brought back from Comet Wild 2
In 2016, scientists reported that the probe Rosetta detected it, along with phosphorus, around Comet 67P
Found in the Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia in 1969
A starting material for heme, the iron-holding part of hemoglobin; its carbons and nitrogen are built into purine rings
One of the most plentiful amino acids made in Stanley Miller’s 1953 spark experiment
Silk fibroin is built mostly from it and alanine; spider silk proteins are also rich in it
Emil Fischer and Ernest Fourneau linked two units of it into the first man-made dipeptide (1901)
Formula C2H5NO2: acetic acid (the acid in vinegar) with an amino group in place of one hydrogen
Swapping one of the two hydrogens on its central carbon for a methyl group gives alanine, the next-simplest amino acid
Collagen’s most common triplet is it, proline, and hydroxyproline; only it fits in the crowded center of the triple helix
Joined to bile acids to make bile salts; with arginine, it is a starting material for creatine

trap.title: Not GABA, not proline
trap.body: Several glycine clues are shared with other answers. GABA is the other main inhibitory neurotransmitter, but it is not one of the 20 amino acids that build proteins. Proline and hydroxyproline also fill collagen’s chains, and alanine is the next-simplest amino acid. Saying just “amino acid” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: The spinal cord, strychnine, every third spot in collagen, a hydrogen side chain, or “the only one that is not chiral” all mean glycine. GABA works mostly in the brain and is made from glutamate; alanine’s side chain is a methyl group.
trap.line: Real answer line: Glycine (accept Gly; prompt on amino acid; do not accept other amino acids)

topics.name: Muscles
topics.kicker: Tissue that contracts to move the body · Skeletal, smooth, and cardiac
topics.dates: More than 600 in the human body
topics.briefing: Every move you make, from blinking to sprinting, comes from muscles, tissues that work by contracting, or getting shorter. Skeletal muscles pull on your bones through tendons, smooth muscles squeeze food through your gut, and cardiac muscle keeps your heart beating your whole life. Inside each muscle cell, protein threads called actin and myosin slide past each other to make the cell shorter.
topics.answerHtml: Muscles (accept muscle tissue or specific types such as skeletal muscle; do not accept “tendons” or “bones”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the 1780s, Luigi Galvani made the legs of dead frogs twitch by touching their nerves with metal tools, and he argued that this tissue held a kind of “animal electricity.” Alessandro Volta disagreed and built the first battery to show that the two metals made the electricity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tissue that contracts to move the body, which comes in skeletal, smooth, and cardiac types.

tossups.p: A. V. Hill shared the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for measuring the heat given off by this tissue as it works. His co-winner, Otto Meyerhof [“MY-er-hoff”], linked the oxygen this tissue uses to the lactic acid it makes.
tossups.r: Tendons connect the skeletal type of this tissue to bones. For 10 points, name this tissue that contracts to move the body.

tossups.p: In 1954, Hugh Huxley and Jean Hanson, and separately Andrew Huxley and Rolf Niedergerke [“NEE-der-gair-kuh”], proposed that thin and thick filaments slide past each other when this tissue contracts. Each repeating unit of the striped, or striated, types of this tissue runs from one Z-disc to the next and is called a sarcomere.
tossups.r: The thin filaments are made of actin, and the thick ones of myosin. For 10 points, name this tissue that contracts to move the body.

tossups.p: John Kendrew won a Nobel Prize for working out the 3D structure of myoglobin, an oxygen-storing protein found in this tissue, the first protein structure ever solved by X-ray crystallography. Slow-twitch fibers of this tissue are packed with myoglobin and mitochondria, which is why a chicken’s legs are dark meat.
tossups.r: Its skeletal type is attached to bones by tendons. For 10 points, name this tissue that comes in skeletal, smooth, and cardiac types.

tossups.p: This tissue’s name comes from the Latin for “little mouse,” supposedly because a bulge of it rippling under the skin looked like a mouse. Cells of the skeletal type of this tissue are long and striped and can each contain hundreds of nuclei.
tossups.r: The biceps and triceps are examples. For 10 points, name these organs that move the body by contracting.

tossups.p: Belgian Blue cattle look extra bulky because a mutation in their gene for myostatin [“my-oh-STAT-in”], a protein that normally limits the growth of this tissue, lets it keep growing. Weight training makes the fibers of this tissue thicker, a change called hypertrophy.
tossups.r: When it goes unused, it shrinks in a process called atrophy. For 10 points, name this tissue whose skeletal type pulls on bones.

tossups.p: Hunters in South America tipped darts with curare [“koo-RAH-ree”], which paralyzes prey by blocking the acetylcholine receptors on this tissue. A single motor neuron and all the fibers of this tissue that it controls are together called a motor unit.
tossups.r: Its skeletal type is controlled voluntarily. For 10 points, name this tissue that contracts to move the body.

tossups.p: When an electrical signal races down the T-tubules of this tissue, a network called the sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium ions. The calcium binds to troponin, which shifts tropomyosin aside so that myosin heads can grab actin and pull.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tissue that contracts to move the body, found in skeletal, smooth, and cardiac forms.

tossups.p: Gap junctions inside structures called intercalated [“in-TER-kuh-lay-ted”] discs let electrical signals spread quickly from cell to cell in one type of this tissue. That type contracts in a steady rhythm set by its own pacemaker cells, without needing signals from the brain.
tossups.r: That type makes up the walls of the heart. For 10 points, name this tissue whose three types are skeletal, smooth, and cardiac.

tossups.p: Tiny arrector pili [“uh-REK-tor PY-lye”], which make hairs stand up as goosebumps, are made of the smooth type of this tissue. That smooth type also forms layers in the walls of the stomach and intestines, pushing food along in waves called peristalsis [“pair-ih-STALL-sis”].
tossups.r: Its skeletal type is attached to bones by tendons. For 10 points, name this tissue that contracts to move the body.

tossups.p: The stapedius [“stuh-PEE-dee-us”], which steadies the tiniest bone in the middle ear, is usually called the smallest skeletal one of these organs. The sartorius [“sar-TOR-ee-us”], which crosses the thigh from the hip to the inside of the knee, is often called the longest.
tossups.r: The gluteus maximus is usually called the largest. For 10 points, name these organs that are attached to bones by tendons.

tossups.p: Titin, the largest known protein in the human body, acts like a spring that lets this tissue bounce back after being stretched. Dystrophin [“dis-TROH-fin”], a protein missing in people with Duchenne [“doo-SHEN”] dystrophy, links the filaments inside this tissue’s cells to their outer membrane.
tossups.r: Actin and myosin filaments slide past each other inside it. For 10 points, name this tissue that contracts to move the body.

tossups.p: After death, cells of this tissue run out of ATP, so their myosin heads stay locked onto actin, causing the stiffness called rigor mortis. During a short sprint, this tissue quickly remakes ATP using energy stored in creatine phosphate.
tossups.r: It contracts to move the body. For 10 points, name this tissue that makes up the biceps and the diaphragm.

tossups.p: During hard exercise, this tissue can turn pyruvate into lactate when oxygen runs low, and the liver turns that lactate back into glucose in a loop named for Carl and Gerty Cori. This tissue stores glucose as glycogen for quick energy.
tossups.r: Its cells contract using actin and myosin. For 10 points, name this tissue whose skeletal type is attached to bones by tendons.

tossups.p: Each skeletal one of these organs is wrapped in a sheath called the epimysium [“ep-ih-MIZ-ee-um”], and the bundles inside it, called fascicles [“FASS-ih-kulz”], are wrapped in perimysium. These organs often work in antagonistic pairs, so that when one contracts, its partner relaxes.
tossups.r: The biceps and triceps form one such pair. For 10 points, name these organs that move the body by contracting.

clues.t: Tissue that contracts (gets shorter) to move the body and its parts
Comes in three types: skeletal, smooth, and cardiac
Skeletal ones are attached to bones by tendons
Examples include the biceps, triceps, quadriceps, and diaphragm
Their cells contract when filaments of actin and myosin slide past each other
Skeletal type: voluntary and striped (striated), with long cells that hold many nuclei
Smooth type: involuntary and not striped; found in the walls of the stomach, intestines, and blood vessels
Cardiac type: striated and found in the heart, its cells linked by intercalated discs with gap junctions
Sliding filament model (1954): thin actin filaments slide past thick myosin filaments in each sarcomere, which runs from Z-disc to Z-disc
Work in antagonistic pairs, like the biceps and triceps: when one contracts, its partner relaxes
A signal travels down T-tubules; calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin, moving tropomyosin aside
Motor neurons trigger them with acetylcholine; one motor neuron plus the fibers it controls is a motor unit
The name comes from the Latin for “little mouse”
The smooth type pushes food through the digestive tract in waves called peristalsis
In the 1780s, Luigi Galvani made dead frogs’ legs twitch and claimed “animal electricity”; Alessandro Volta disagreed and built the first battery
A. V. Hill (heat) and Otto Meyerhof (oxygen use and lactic acid) shared the 1922 Nobel Prize for studying them
Hugh Huxley and Jean Hanson, and separately Andrew Huxley and Rolf Niedergerke, proposed the sliding filament model
Myoglobin, their oxygen-storing protein, was the first protein whose structure was solved by X-ray crystallography (John Kendrew)
Slow-twitch fibers, rich in myoglobin and mitochondria, resist tiring (dark meat); fast-twitch fibers give quick bursts
A myostatin mutation makes Belgian Blue cattle extra bulky; training causes hypertrophy and disuse causes atrophy
Curare on South American hunting darts blocks their acetylcholine receptors, causing paralysis
The stapedius is usually called the smallest skeletal one, the sartorius the longest, and the gluteus maximus the largest
Titin, the largest known human protein, acts as a spring; dystrophin, missing in Duchenne dystrophy, anchors their filaments
Without ATP after death, myosin stays stuck to actin (rigor mortis); creatine phosphate quickly remakes ATP during sprints
During hard exercise they make lactate, which the liver turns back into glucose (Cori cycle); they store glucose as glycogen
Arrector pili, tiny smooth ones, raise hairs to make goosebumps
Each skeletal one is wrapped in epimysium; the bundles inside, called fascicles, are wrapped in perimysium

trap.title: Not the tendon or bone
trap.body: Many clues describe how muscles pull on the skeleton, so players blurt the parts being pulled. Tendons connect muscles to bones, ligaments connect bones to other bones, and bones are the levers that get moved. Clues about actin and myosin can also tempt a player to name a protein instead of the tissue.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this tissue” that contracts, or names skeletal, smooth, and cardiac types, say “muscles.” Tough cords that attach it to bone are tendons, and links between two bones are ligaments.
trap.line: Real answer line: Muscles (accept muscle tissue; do not accept “tendons” or “bones”)

topics.name: Human evolution
topics.kicker: How our species arose from earlier primates · Traced through fossils and DNA
topics.briefing: Human evolution is the story of how our species, Homo sapiens, arose from earlier primates over roughly 7 million years. Fossils like “Lucy,” a 3.2-million-year-old skeleton found in Ethiopia in 1974, show that our ancestors walked upright long before their brains grew large. Most scientists agree that modern humans first appeared in Africa and later spread across the world, meeting Neanderthals along the way.
topics.answerHtml: Human evolution (accept evolution of humans or hominin evolution; prompt on evolution; do not accept “Neanderthals”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ethiopians call a skeleton found at Hadar in 1974 Dinkinesh [“din-KEE-nesh”], meaning “you are marvelous,” but its English nickname comes from a Beatles song that played at the discoverers’ camp. Donald Johanson’s team found that partial skeleton, an Australopithecus afarensis about 3.2 million years old.
tossups.r: That skeleton is nicknamed “Lucy.” For 10 points, name this process, studied by paleoanthropologists, by which our species arose from earlier primates.

tossups.p: Volcanic ash at Laetoli [“lay-TOH-lee”], Tanzania, preserved a trail of footprints about 3.6 million years old, showing that some early hominins walked upright long before their brains grew large. Mary Leakey’s team uncovered those footprints in the late 1970s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, illustrated by fossils like “Lucy,” in which modern people arose from earlier hominins.

tossups.p: In 1959, Mary Leakey found the skull of a big-toothed hominin nicknamed “Nutcracker Man” at Olduvai [“OHL-duh-vy”] Gorge in Tanzania. Her family later found fossils of Homo habilis, the “handy man,” there, near simple stone tools called Oldowan tools.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process by which Homo sapiens arose from earlier primates, a story that fossils like “Lucy” help tell.

tossups.p: In 1891, Eugène Dubois [“oo-ZHEN doo-BWAH”] found “Java Man” in Indonesia, and in the 1920s, scientists dug up “Peking Man” near Beijing, though most of those Chinese fossils were lost in 1941. Both finds belong to Homo erectus, which made teardrop-shaped Acheulean [“uh-SHOO-lee-un”] hand axes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, studied through fossils like “Lucy,” by which our species arose from earlier primates.

tossups.p: In 1984, Kamoya Kimeu, working with Richard Leakey’s team, found the nearly complete skeleton of a Homo erectus youth near Lake Turkana in Kenya. Homo erectus was probably the first hominin to spread out of Africa, reaching places as far away as Indonesia.
tossups.r: That skeleton is the “Turkana Boy.” For 10 points, name this process by which modern people arose from earlier hominins.

tossups.p: In 1925, Raymond Dart described the “Taung Child,” a young fossil skull from South Africa, and named its species Australopithecus africanus, meaning “southern ape from Africa.” For years, many experts rejected Dart’s claim that the skull belonged to one of our early relatives.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, studied by paleoanthropologists, by which Homo sapiens arose from earlier primates.

tossups.p: Fossils found in a gravel pit at Piltdown, England, in 1912 fooled many scientists for decades, until tests in 1953 proved them a hoax made from a person’s skull and an orangutan’s jaw. That fake “missing link” had distracted researchers studying this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, studied through real fossils like “Lucy,” in which our species arose from earlier primates.

tossups.p: The multiregional hypothesis says that modern people developed from older hominin groups in several parts of the world, linked by interbreeding. Its main rival says Homo sapiens arose in Africa and later spread across the world, an idea supported by studies of mitochondrial DNA.
tossups.r: That rival is the “Out of Africa” model. For 10 points, name this process, by which our species arose from earlier primates.

tossups.p: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud [“JEB-ul eer-HOOD”] in Morocco, announced in 2017, pushed the oldest known remains of Homo sapiens back to about 300,000 years ago. Before that, skulls found near the Omo River in Ethiopia had been the oldest known.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, illustrated by fossils like “Lucy,” through which our species arose from earlier primates.

tossups.p: People have 46 chromosomes while chimpanzees have 48, because two ancestral chromosomes fused end to end to form our chromosome 2. Comparing the two species’ genomes shows that their DNA is more than 98 percent identical.
tossups.r: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives. For 10 points, name this process by which Homo sapiens arose from earlier primates.

tossups.p: In his 1871 book _The Descent of Man_, Charles Darwin predicted that people most likely first arose in Africa, because gorillas and chimpanzees live there. Eight years earlier, Thomas Henry Huxley had compared the skeletons of people and apes in _Evidence as to Man’s Place in Nature_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, studied through fossils like “Lucy,” in which modern people arose from earlier hominins.

tossups.p: A skull nicknamed Toumaï [“too-MY”], found in Chad in 2001 by Michel Brunet’s team, may be one of the oldest known hominins, at about 7 million years old. Ardi, a skeleton of Ardipithecus from Ethiopia described in 2009, lived about 4.4 million years ago.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process by which Homo sapiens arose from earlier primates over millions of years.

tossups.p: Lee Berger’s team announced Homo naledi [“nah-LEH-dee”] in 2015 after recovering its fossils from deep inside the Rising Star cave system in South Africa. Eleven years earlier, scientists described a tiny species nicknamed the “hobbit,” Homo floresiensis, from the island of Flores in Indonesia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, studied by paleoanthropologists, in which modern people arose from earlier hominins.

tossups.p: Svante Pääbo [“SVAHN-teh PAY-boh”] won the 2022 Nobel Prize for ancient-DNA research showing that early modern people had children with Neanderthals and with Denisovans, a group first identified from a finger bone in a Siberian cave. Most people with ancestors from outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA.
tossups.r: The Laetoli footprints and the skeleton “Lucy” are famous evidence of this process. For 10 points, name this process by which our species arose from earlier primates.

tossups.p: The foramen magnum [“for-AY-men MAG-num”], the hole where the spinal cord enters the skull, sits farther forward in species that walk upright. The hip and leg bones of a skeleton found in Ethiopia in 1974 showed that it walked on two legs, though its brain was about the size of a chimpanzee’s.
tossups.r: That skeleton is “Lucy,” found by Donald Johanson’s team. For 10 points, name this process by which modern people arose from earlier hominins.

clues.t: The process by which our species, Homo sapiens, arose from earlier primates over millions of years
“Lucy,” a 3.2-million-year-old _Australopithecus afarensis_ skeleton, was found in Ethiopia in 1974 by Donald Johanson’s team
“Out of Africa”: Homo sapiens first arose in Africa and later spread across the world

The Leakey family (Louis, Mary, Richard, and Meave) found many key fossils in East Africa
Walking upright on two legs (bipedalism) came long before big brains
The Laetoli footprints in Tanzania, about 3.6 million years old and preserved in volcanic ash, were uncovered by Mary Leakey’s team
_Homo habilis_ (“handy man”) is linked to simple Oldowan stone tools found at Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania
_Homo erectus_ (“upright man”) made Acheulean hand axes and was probably the first hominin to leave Africa

Our species and its extinct close relatives are called hominins
The multiregional hypothesis, the main rival to “Out of Africa,” says modern people developed in several regions at once
Mitochondrial DNA traces all living people back to a “Mitochondrial Eve” who lived in Africa
Charles Darwin’s _The Descent of Man_ (1871) predicted that people first arose in Africa
Lucy is called Dinkinesh (“you are marvelous”) in Amharic; her English name comes from a Beatles song played at camp
Java Man (Eugène Dubois, 1891) and Peking Man (China, 1920s) are _Homo erectus_; most Peking Man fossils were lost in 1941
Kamoya Kimeu found the Turkana Boy, a nearly complete _Homo erectus_ skeleton, in Kenya in 1984
Raymond Dart described the Taung Child (1925) and named _Australopithecus africanus_, “southern ape from Africa”
Mary Leakey found the big-toothed “Nutcracker Man” at Olduvai Gorge in 1959
Piltdown Man (England, 1912) was exposed in 1953 as a hoax: a person’s skull with an orangutan’s jaw
Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco (announced 2017), are the oldest known _Homo sapiens_, about 300,000 years old
Our chromosome 2 formed when two ancestral chromosomes fused, so people have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees have 48
Thomas Henry Huxley compared the skeletons of people and apes in _Evidence as to Man’s Place in Nature_ (1863)
Toumaï (Chad, found 2001, about 7 million years old) may be one of the oldest known hominins; Ardi (_Ardipithecus_, Ethiopia, described 2009) lived about 4.4 million years ago
_Homo naledi_ (Rising Star cave, South Africa, 2015) and the tiny “hobbit,” _Homo floresiensis_ (Flores, Indonesia, 2004)
Svante Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize for ancient-DNA work showing interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans
A foramen magnum (where the spinal cord enters the skull) that sits farther forward shows a species walked upright

trap.title: The process, not a fossil
trap.body: Human evolution tossups are packed with famous fossils and species, like Lucy, _Homo erectus_, and the Neanderthals, and each of those is its own answer line. A player who blurts the name of a fossil or species when the question asks for “this process” gets it wrong. Saying just “evolution” is on the right track but earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen to the last line: “this process” plus fossils, hominins, or our species wants human evolution. “This species” or “these hominins” wants a specific group, like the Neanderthals. If you hear only general Darwin clues, like finches and natural selection, the answer may be plain evolution instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Human evolution (accept evolution of humans; prompt on evolution; do not accept “Neanderthals”)

topics.name: B vitamins
topics.kicker: Eight water-soluble vitamins · From thiamine (B1) to cobalamin (B12)
topics.briefing: The B vitamins are a family of eight water-soluble vitamins that help your cells turn food into energy, mostly by helping enzymes do their jobs. Many have names as well as numbers: thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), folate (B9), and cobalamin (B12). Lacking one can cause a disease, such as beriberi without thiamine or pellagra without niacin, which is how scientists first discovered them.
topics.answerHtml: B vitamins (accept vitamin B complex; prompt on vitamins; do not accept a single B vitamin or “vitamin C”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the 1890s in Java, Christiaan Eijkman [“AYK-mahn”] noticed that chickens fed polished white rice developed a nerve disease, while chickens fed unpolished rice stayed healthy. Eijkman shared the 1929 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work that pointed to a missing nutrient from this group.
tossups.r: That nutrient, thiamine, prevents beriberi. For 10 points, name this group of water-soluble vitamins that also includes niacin and folic acid.

tossups.p: In 1937, Conrad Elvehjem [“EL-vuh-yem”] found that one of these vitamins cured “black tongue” in dogs. Two decades earlier, Joseph Goldberger had shown that pellagra, a similar disease that caused rough skin rashes across the American South, came from a poor diet rather than from germs.
tossups.r: That vitamin is niacin. For 10 points, name this family of water-soluble vitamins that also includes thiamine and cobalamin.

tossups.p: Cooks in Mexico and Central America have long soaked corn in limewater before grinding it, a process called nixtamalization [“nish-tuh-mah-lee-ZAY-shun”] that frees one of these vitamins so the body can absorb it. Where people ate untreated corn as their main food, a lack of that vitamin caused pellagra.
tossups.r: That vitamin is niacin. For 10 points, name this group of eight water-soluble vitamins, which also includes thiamine and riboflavin.

tossups.p: George Minot and William Murphy shared the 1934 Nobel Prize with George Whipple after they treated pernicious anemia by feeding patients large amounts of liver, which is rich in one of these vitamins. That vitamin is the only vitamin that contains a metal atom: cobalt.
tossups.r: That vitamin, cobalamin, is number 12 in this group. For 10 points, name this group of water-soluble vitamins that also includes thiamine.

tossups.p: In the 1950s, Dorothy Hodgkin used X-ray crystallography to work out the structure of one of these vitamins, part of the work that earned her the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Robert Woodward and Albert Eschenmoser [“ESH-en-moh-zer”] later led a huge team that built that same molecule from scratch, finishing in 1972.
tossups.r: That vitamin, cobalamin, contains cobalt. For 10 points, name this family of water-soluble vitamins that includes thiamine and niacin.

tossups.p: Only bacteria and archaea can make one of these vitamins, so it is found naturally almost only in animal foods. Absorbing that vitamin requires intrinsic factor, a protein made in the stomach, and losing that protein leads to pernicious anemia.
tossups.r: That vitamin is cobalamin. For 10 points, name this group of vitamins, numbered from 1 to 12, that includes thiamine and folic acid.

tossups.p: Avidin, a protein in raw egg whites, grabs onto biotin, one of these vitamins, so tightly that scientists use the pair as a molecular “glue.” Biotin was once called vitamin H, and the body uses it to help enzymes build fats.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of water-soluble vitamins whose other members include thiamine, niacin, and cobalamin.

tossups.p: Pantothenic [“pan-toh-THEN-ik”] acid, one of these vitamins, takes its name from a Greek word meaning “from everywhere,” because nearly every food contains some. The body uses it to build coenzyme A, which carries pieces of food molecules into the Krebs cycle.
tossups.r: Other members of this group include riboflavin and folic acid. For 10 points, name this family of water-soluble vitamins.

tossups.p: One of these vitamins is a yellow-orange compound whose name partly comes from the Latin word for “yellow,” and extra amounts of it can turn urine bright yellow. The body uses that vitamin to build FAD, a molecule that carries electrons during cellular respiration.
tossups.r: That vitamin is riboflavin. For 10 points, name this group of water-soluble vitamins that includes thiamine and niacin.

tossups.p: Around 1930, Lucy Wills found that Marmite, a yeast extract, could cure a type of anemia in pregnant textile workers in Bombay, India. The nutrient behind her discovery turned out to be one of these vitamins, which the body needs in order to make DNA.
tossups.r: That vitamin is folate, or folic acid. For 10 points, name this group of water-soluble vitamins that also includes thiamine.

tossups.p: One of these vitamins is named for the Latin word for “leaf,” since it was first isolated from spinach leaves. Since the late 1990s, that vitamin has been added to flour and other grain products in the United States to lower the rate of neural tube defects such as spina bifida [“SPY-nuh BIF-ih-duh”].
tossups.r: That vitamin is folic acid. For 10 points, name this group of vitamins that also includes thiamine and cobalamin.

tossups.p: In 1912, while studying a substance in rice bran that prevents beriberi, the Polish biochemist Casimir Funk coined the word “vitamine,” short for “vital amine.” That anti-beriberi substance was the first member of this group to be discovered.
tossups.r: That substance is thiamine. For 10 points, name this group of water-soluble vitamins that also includes niacin and riboflavin.

tossups.p: Pyridoxine [“peer-ih-DOK-seen”], one of these vitamins, helps enzymes process amino acids, including a step in turning tryptophan into the messenger chemical serotonin. Its active form, called PLP, helps more than 100 different enzymes do their jobs.
tossups.r: Gaps in this group’s numbering come from substances that turned out not to be vitamins. For 10 points, name this group that includes thiamine and niacin.

tossups.p: Sulfa drugs stop many bacteria from growing by blocking how they make one of these vitamins, while the cancer drug methotrexate [“meth-oh-TREK-sayt”] blocks how cells use that same vitamin. A lack of either that vitamin or another member of this group causes anemia with oversized red blood cells.
tossups.r: Those two vitamins are folate and cobalamin. For 10 points, name this group of water-soluble vitamins that includes thiamine.

tossups.p: In 1941, the United States began “enriching” white flour with iron and three of these vitamins, replacing nutrients lost when wheat is milled. Milling brown rice into white rice also strips away the bran, which holds much of these vitamins.
tossups.r: Yeast extracts such as Marmite and Vegemite are rich in them. For 10 points, name this group of vitamins that includes thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin.

Avidin in raw egg whites grabs biotin tightly; biotin, once called vitamin H, helps enzymes build fats
Pantothenic acid’s name means “from everywhere,” since nearly every food has some; the body builds coenzyme A from it
