trap.title: One vitamin, or the family?
trap.body: Tossups on this group often spend their early clues on one member, like thiamine and beriberi, or cobalamin and pernicious anemia. A player who buzzes with that single vitamin is wrong when the question wants the whole group. Vitamin C, the only other water-soluble vitamin, is another common wrong answer, and saying just “vitamins” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Wait for the noun: “this group,” “this family,” or “these vitamins” wants the B vitamins, while “this vitamin” wants one member. Scurvy, citrus fruit, and collagen mean vitamin C, not this group.
trap.line: Real answer line: B vitamins (accept vitamin B complex; prompt on vitamins; do not accept a single B vitamin)

topics.name: Vacuoles
topics.kicker: Membrane-bound storage sacs · Keep plant cells firm with turgor pressure
topics.dates: Can fill about 90 percent of a plant cell
topics.briefing: Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs that cells use like storage closets for water, food, pigments, and waste. In a plant cell, one huge central vacuole can fill about 90 percent of the space, and its water pushes outward against the cell wall to keep the plant firm; when it runs low, the plant wilts. Some single-celled organisms use contractile vacuoles to pump out extra water so they don’t burst.
topics.answerHtml: Vacuoles (accept central vacuole, contractile vacuole, or food vacuole; do not accept “vesicles” or “lysosomes”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Yoshinori Ohsumi [“oh-SOO-mee”] won the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine after watching yeast cells send worn-out parts into this organelle to be broken down, a process called autophagy [“aw-TOFF-uh-jee”]. In plants and fungi, this organelle does much of the digesting that lysosomes do in animal cells.
tossups.r: In plant cells, a large central one stores water. For 10 points, name this membrane-bound storage organelle.

tossups.p: Pumps called V-type ATPases in the tonoplast [“TOH-nuh-plast”], the membrane around this organelle, push hydrogen ions inside and keep this organelle acidic. Water channels called aquaporins in the tonoplast let water flow quickly into and out of this organelle.
tossups.r: A plant cell’s large central one pushes water against the cell wall. For 10 points, name this storage organelle.

tossups.p: The leaves of the sensitive plant Mimosa pudica [“mih-MOH-suh PYOO-dih-kuh”] fold up when touched because cells at their bases quickly lose water from this organelle. Plant cells grow larger cheaply by filling this organelle with water instead of building more cytoplasm.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle, which in plant cells is a large central sac that creates turgor pressure.

tossups.p: Cacti and pineapples, which use CAM photosynthesis, store carbon dioxide overnight as malic acid inside this organelle. The purple pigment in red cabbage that students use to test acids and bases is also stored in this organelle.
tossups.r: Its large central version in plant cells pushes against the cell wall, creating turgor pressure. For 10 points, name this storage organelle.

tossups.p: In Paramecium [“pair-uh-MEE-see-um”], star-shaped versions of this organelle collect extra water through canals that spread out like spokes, then squeeze it out of the cell so the cell does not burst. An amoeba forms another kind of this organelle around each bit of food it swallows.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these membrane-bound sacs, including the large central one that stores water in plant cells.

tossups.p: Lazzaro Spallanzani [“spahl-lahn-TSAH-nee”] saw star-shaped examples of this structure in single-celled organisms in 1776 but mistook them for breathing organs, and Félix Dujardin [“doo-zhar-DAN”] named them in 1841. In 1885, Hugo de Vries named this structure’s membrane the tonoplast.
tossups.r: Its name comes from the Latin for “empty.” For 10 points, name this organelle, which in plant cells is a large central water-filled sac.

tossups.p: When a plant cell sits in very salty water, this organelle loses water by osmosis and shrinks, so the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall in a process called plasmolysis [“plaz-MOL-ih-sis”]. Students often watch this happen in red onion skin cells, whose purple pigment sits inside this organelle.
tossups.r: When it runs low on water, a plant wilts. For 10 points, name this organelle, which is large and central in plant cells.

tossups.p: Needle-shaped crystals of calcium oxalate, which make some plants painful to chew, often form inside this organelle. In seeds, special versions of this organelle hold stored proteins that a sprouting seedling breaks down for food.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this membrane-bound storage organelle, which in plant cells is a large central sac full of water.

tossups.p: When guard cells pump potassium ions into this organelle, water follows by osmosis, the guard cells swell, and the stoma between them opens. When the guard cells lose water from this organelle, they go limp and the stoma closes.
tossups.r: In a mature plant cell, the central one can fill about 90 percent of the space. For 10 points, name this organelle.

tossups.p: When an amoeba engulfs a meal by phagocytosis [“fag-oh-sy-TOH-sis”], the food ends up inside one of these organelles, which then fuses with lysosomes that digest it. Freshwater protists use a contractile kind of this organelle to pump out extra water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organelles, whose large central version stores water in plant cells.

tossups.p: Many plants that grow in salty soil pump extra sodium ions into this organelle, keeping the salt away from the enzymes in the rest of the cell. Yeast cells use their version of this organelle to store amino acids and phosphate.
tossups.r: A plant cell’s large central one keeps the plant firm. For 10 points, name this membrane-bound storage organelle.

tossups.p: Cassava and many other plants keep defense chemicals inside this organelle, away from the enzymes that turn them poisonous, so the poison forms only when an animal chews the plant. Proteins headed for this organelle are sorted in the Golgi apparatus.
tossups.r: Water flowing back into the central one makes wilted lettuce crisp again. For 10 points, name this organelle.

tossups.p: Sugarcane and sugar beets store the sucrose that people turn into table sugar inside this organelle. Grapes and other fruits also keep their sugars and acids dissolved in this organelle’s watery fluid, called cell sap.
tossups.r: Its central version can fill most of a plant cell. For 10 points, name this membrane-bound storage organelle.

tossups.p: Lemons taste sour because their juice cells store citric acid inside this organelle, making it one of the most acidic spaces found in any plant. This organelle also holds digestive enzymes that break down worn-out cell parts, much like a lysosome.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle, which in plant cells is a large central sac that stores water.

tossups.p: Gardeners can turn some hydrangea flowers blue by making the soil more acidic, which lets aluminum reach the pigments stored in this organelle. Some morning glory flowers turn from purple to blue as they open, because the inside of this organelle becomes less acidic.
tossups.r: Its central version in plant cells creates turgor pressure. For 10 points, name this membrane-bound storage organelle.

clues.t: A membrane-bound sac that stores water, food, pigments, and wastes
Plant cells have one large central one that can fill about 90 percent of the cell
Its water pushes against the cell wall, creating turgor pressure that keeps plants firm
When it loses water, the plant wilts
Animal cells have only small ones, if any
Its membrane is called the tonoplast
Its watery fluid is called cell sap, which holds sugars, salts, acids, and pigments
Contractile ones in freshwater protists, like _Paramecium_, pump out extra water so the cell does not burst
Food ones form when an amoeba engulfs food by phagocytosis, then fuse with lysosomes for digestion
In salty water it loses water and shrinks, and the cell membrane pulls away from the wall: plasmolysis
In plants and fungi it does much of the digesting that lysosomes do in animal cells, and its inside is acidic
Water moves into and out of it by osmosis, which is why wilted lettuce gets crisp again in water
Its name comes from the Latin word for “empty”
Yoshinori Ohsumi won the 2016 Nobel Prize for studying autophagy, in which yeast send worn-out parts into it to be broken down
V-type ATPase pumps in the tonoplast push hydrogen ions in; aquaporins let water through
_Mimosa pudica_ leaves fold when touched because cells at their bases lose water from it
Guard cells pump potassium ions into it; water follows, the guard cells swell, and the stoma opens
CAM plants like cacti and pineapples store carbon dioxide in it overnight as malic acid
It stores anthocyanins, the red, purple, and blue pigments of red cabbage, red onions, and many flowers
Spallanzani saw star-shaped ones in 1776; Félix Dujardin named them in 1841; Hugo de Vries named the tonoplast in 1885
Needle-like calcium oxalate crystals often form in it; seeds keep stored proteins in special ones
Plant cells grow larger cheaply by filling it with water instead of building more cytoplasm
Many salt-tolerant plants pump sodium ions into it; yeast store amino acids and phosphate in theirs
Cassava keeps defense chemicals in it, apart from the enzymes that make them poisonous; its proteins are sorted in the Golgi
Sugarcane and sugar beets store sucrose in it; lemons store citric acid in it, making it extremely acidic
Blue hydrangeas get their color when aluminum reaches pigments in it; morning glories turn blue as it becomes less acidic

trap.title: Vacuole, vesicle, or lysosome?
trap.body: Vacuoles, vesicles, and lysosomes are all membrane-wrapped sacs, so their clues overlap. Vesicles are tiny shipping bubbles that carry materials between organelles, and lysosomes are digestive sacs in animal cells. Plant vacuoles even do a lysosome’s digesting job, so clues about breaking down old cell parts can point either way.
trap.fix: Plants, the cell wall, turgor pressure, wilting, the tonoplast, or Paramecium pumping out water mean vacuoles. Tiny bubbles moving between the ER and the Golgi are vesicles; digestive sacs in animal cells, with clues about Christian de Duve, mean lysosomes.
trap.line: Real answer line: Vacuoles (accept central vacuole or contractile vacuole; do not accept “vesicles” or “lysosomes”)

topics.name: Sponges
topics.kicker: Phylum Porifera, the simplest animals · Filter food from water through pores
topics.dates: Among the oldest animal groups on Earth
topics.briefing: Sponges look like plants, but they are animals, and among the simplest ones alive: no brain, no heart, no stomach, and no true tissues or organs. Their bodies are full of tiny pores, which is why their phylum is called Porifera, or “pore bearers.” Special collar cells with whip-like flagella pull water through those pores, and the sponge filters out bits of food. Natural bath sponges are the dried skeletons of some kinds.
topics.answerHtml: Sponges (accept Porifera or poriferans; do not accept “cnidarians” or “corals”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1907, Henry Van Peters Wilson squeezed one of these animals through fine silk cloth to separate its cells, and the loose cells crawled back together into a new animal. These animals have several kinds of specialized cells, but no true tissues or organs.
tossups.r: Most are filter feeders that live on the seafloor. For 10 points, name these simple animals whose bodies are full of pores.

tossups.p: The collar cells, or choanocytes [“koh-AN-uh-sites”], that line the inner chambers of these animals look almost exactly like single-celled choanoflagellates, the closest living relatives of all animals. Each collar cell beats a whip-like flagellum to keep water moving through these animals.
tossups.r: Water enters through many small pores and leaves through an opening called the osculum. For 10 points, name these filter-feeding animals.

tossups.p: Glassy members of this group build six-rayed spicules [“SPIK-yoolz”] out of silica, while chalky members build their spicules from calcium carbonate. Most species of these animals have skeletons made of silica spicules, a tough collagen protein, or both.
tossups.r: Dried skeletons of some kinds are used for bathing. For 10 points, name these simple, pore-covered animals.

tossups.p: A pair of shrimp often spends its whole life trapped inside the glassy skeleton of the Venus’s flower basket, one of these animals, which is given as a wedding gift in Japan as a symbol of lasting love. Fibers in that skeleton carry light much like fiber-optic cables.
tossups.r: They have no brain, heart, or stomach. For 10 points, name these simple filter-feeding animals, whose bodies are full of pores.

tossups.p: Robert Grant, an early mentor of Charles Darwin, watched water currents flowing through these animals in the 1820s and later coined the scientific name of their phylum. For centuries before that, many naturalists had thought these animals were plants.
tossups.r: That name means “pore bearer.” For 10 points, name these simple animals, some of whose skeletons are used as bath scrubbers.

tossups.p: The harp-shaped Chondrocladia lyra [“kon-droh-KLAY-dee-uh LY-ruh”], described from deep water off California in 2012, is a meat-eating member of this group that snags tiny crustaceans with hook-covered branches. Those hooks work a bit like Velcro.
tossups.r: Most members of this group instead filter food from water pumped through their pores. For 10 points, name these simple animals.

tossups.p: Freshwater members of this group survive freezing winters and droughts by forming gemmules [“JEM-yoolz”], tough little packets of cells that grow into new animals when conditions improve. Many members of this group are hermaphrodites, meaning that one individual makes both eggs and sperm.
tossups.r: Adults stay fixed in one place. For 10 points, name these pore-filled animals, which have no true tissues or organs.

tossups.p: Biologists sort the body plans of these animals into asconoid [“ASS-kuh-noyd”], syconoid [“SY-kuh-noyd”], and leuconoid [“LOO-kuh-noyd”] types, from simplest to most complex. In all three types, water enters through tiny pores called ostia [“OSS-tee-uh”]. Most species have the leuconoid type, with many small chambers lined by collar cells.
tossups.r: Water leaves through a large opening called the osculum. For 10 points, name these simple filter-feeding animals.

tossups.p: Wandering amoebocytes [“uh-MEE-buh-sites”] in the jelly-like mesohyl [“MEZ-uh-hyl”] of these animals carry food to other cells and can turn into other cell types. Some of those wandering cells also build the tiny skeletal pieces called spicules. Flat cells called pinacocytes [“pin-AK-uh-sites”] form the outer covering of these animals.
tossups.r: Collar cells called choanocytes pull water through these animals’ pores. For 10 points, name these simple animals.

tossups.p: The cancer drug cytarabine [“sy-TAIR-uh-been”] was developed from chemicals first found in a Caribbean member of this group in the 1950s. In the early 1900s, Greek immigrant divers made Tarpon Springs, Florida, famous for harvesting these animals.
tossups.r: Their dried skeletons were sold for bathing and cleaning. For 10 points, name these simple, pore-filled animals.

tossups.p: Chemical traces in rocks more than 600 million years old may have been left by these animals, which many scientists place on the oldest branch of the animal family tree. Comb jellies are their main rivals for that title.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these simple filter feeders, whose bodies are full of pores and which have no true tissues.

tossups.p: Boring members of this group, such as Cliona [“KLY-oh-nuh”], use chemicals to dissolve tunnels into oyster shells and coral. In some members of this group, bacteria living inside the body make up as much as a third of its weight.
tossups.r: Most are filter feeders whose collar cells pull water through many tiny pores. For 10 points, name these simple animals.

tossups.p: Reefs built by glass-skeleton members of this group, once known only from fossils, were found alive off the coast of British Columbia in the 1980s. Some glass members of this group may live for thousands of years.
tossups.r: Most of them filter food from seawater. For 10 points, name these pore-covered animals, which have no brain, heart, or stomach.

tossups.p: In the simplest members of this group, tube-shaped cells called porocytes [“POR-uh-sites”] form the openings through which water enters. Water then flows into a central cavity and out through one large opening at the top. These animals digest food inside individual cells.
tossups.r: That opening is the osculum. For 10 points, name these simple animals whose bodies are full of pores.

tossups.p: Members of this group release swimming larvae with names like amphiblastula [“am-fee-BLAST-yoo-luh”] and parenchymella [“puh-ren-kih-MEL-uh”], which use cilia to move for a short time before settling down for good. Pieces broken off these animals can also regrow into whole new animals.
tossups.r: Adults stay attached to one spot and filter food from water. For 10 points, name these simple, pore-filled animals.

Their collar cells look like choanoflagellates, the single-celled closest living relatives of animals
Glass members (class Hexactinellida) have six-rayed silica spicules; chalky members (class Calcarea) use calcium carbonate
With no gut, they digest food inside individual cells
Freshwater ones survive winter and drought as gemmules, packets of cells that grow into new animals
In 1907, H. V. Wilson squeezed one through silk cloth; the separated cells crawled back together into a new animal
The glassy Venus’s flower basket often traps a pair of shrimp and is a wedding gift in Japan; its fibers carry light like fiber optics
Robert Grant, an early mentor of Charles Darwin, studied their water currents in the 1820s and later named their phylum
Some deep-sea ones eat meat, like the harp-shaped _Chondrocladia lyra_ (described 2012), which snags crustaceans with hooks
Many are hermaphrodites: one individual makes both eggs and sperm
Body plans are asconoid, syconoid, and leuconoid, from simplest to most complex; most species are leuconoid
Amoebocytes wander through the jelly-like mesohyl, carrying food and making spicules; flat pinacocytes cover the outside
The cancer drug cytarabine was developed from chemicals first found in a Caribbean one in the 1950s
Greek immigrant divers made Tarpon Springs, Florida, famous for harvesting them in the early 1900s
Many scientists put them on the oldest branch of the animal family tree, though comb jellies rival them
Boring ones like _Cliona_ dissolve tunnels in shells and coral; bacteria can make up a third of some species’ weight
Reefs of glass ones, once known only from fossils, were found alive off British Columbia in the 1980s; some may live thousands of years
In the simplest ones, tube-shaped porocytes form the openings where water enters
Their swimming larvae have names like amphiblastula and parenchymella

trap.title: Not a cnidarian
trap.body: Sponges and cnidarians (corals, jellyfish, and sea anemones) often appear side by side in questions about simple sea animals, and both can be stuck to rocks and reefs. But cnidarians have true tissues, a gut, and stinging cells, while sponges have none of these. Loofahs, the scrubbers sold in bath shops, come from a plant, not an animal.
trap.fix: Pores, collar cells (choanocytes), spicules, spongin, an osculum, or “no true tissues” mean sponges. Stinging cells (cnidocytes or nematocysts), tentacles, polyps, and medusas mean cnidarians.
trap.line: Real answer line: Sponges (accept Porifera; do not accept “cnidarians” or “corals”)

topics.name: Lac operon
topics.kicker: E. coli genes for digesting lactose · The classic case of gene control
topics.briefing: The lac operon is a set of three genes that lets the gut bacterium E. coli digest lactose, the sugar in milk. Most of the time a repressor protein sits on the DNA and keeps the genes switched off, but when lactose shows up, it pulls the repressor away and the genes turn on. François Jacob and Jacques Monod figured this out in 1961 and won a Nobel Prize, giving biologists their first clear picture of how genes are switched on and off.
topics.answerHtml: Lac operon (accept lactose operon; prompt on operon; do not accept “trp operon”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A French biologist’s doctoral research found that E. coli fed a mix of two sugars grows in two separate spurts, a pattern he called diauxie [“dy-AWK-see”], because the bacteria use up the glucose before switching on this set of genes. The two spurts are separated by a pause while the bacteria build new enzymes.
tossups.r: That biologist, Jacques Monod, later explained these genes with François Jacob. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes that is switched on by lactose.

tossups.p: In the 1959 “PaJaMo” experiment, named for its three scientists, bacterial mating showed that one gene in this system makes a substance that can travel through the cell and shut the other genes off. Arthur Pardee supplied the “Pa” in that experiment’s name.
tossups.r: The other syllables stand for François Jacob and Jacques Monod. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes for digesting lactose.

tossups.p: In 1966, Walter Gilbert and Benno Müller-Hill became the first scientists to isolate a repressor protein, the one that controls this set of genes. That repressor shuts these genes off by sitting on a stretch of DNA called the operator, where it blocks RNA polymerase.
tossups.r: Lactose removes that repressor and switches these genes on. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes studied by Jacob and Monod.

tossups.p: In blue-white screening, scientists insert new DNA into the middle of a gene from this system, so bacterial colonies that carry the new DNA stay white on dishes containing X-gal instead of turning blue. Lab workers often switch these genes on with IPTG, a look-alike of the natural trigger that bacteria cannot break down.
tossups.r: Its Z gene makes beta-galactosidase. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes that is switched on by lactose.

tossups.p: The three main genes of this system, labeled Z, Y, and A, code for beta-galactosidase [“BAY-tuh guh-lak-TOH-sih-dayss”], a permease that carries sugar into the cell, and a transacetylase [“trans-uh-SEE-tuh-layss”]. Beta-galactosidase splits a sugar into glucose and galactose.
tossups.r: That sugar is lactose. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes explained by François Jacob and Jacques Monod.

tossups.p: The true trigger for this system is allolactose [“al-oh-LAK-tohss”], a rearranged form of a sugar, which binds the repressor and changes its shape so that it lets go of the DNA. Because binding a small molecule changes its shape, that repressor is called an allosteric protein.
tossups.r: That form comes from lactose. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes studied by Jacob and Monod.

tossups.p: “Constitutive” mutants of this system make its enzymes all the time, even without the sugar that normally switches it on. Bacteria carrying two copies of these genes showed that the operator controls only the genes on its own stretch of DNA, while the repressor can act from anywhere in the cell.
tossups.r: Jacob and Monod explained these genes. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes that is switched on by lactose.

tossups.p: When glucose is plentiful, levels of cyclic AMP drop, so the catabolite activator protein, or CAP, cannot attach near this system’s promoter and boost it, an effect called catabolite repression. As a result, these genes work hardest only when glucose is absent.
tossups.r: They also need lactose to be present. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes studied by Jacob and Monod.

tossups.p: One of the two scientists who explained this system wrote the 1970 book _Chance and Necessity_, and the other wrote _The Logic of Life_. Both men fought against Nazi Germany in World War II, one in the French Resistance and the other with the Free French forces.
tossups.r: Those scientists were Jacques Monod and François Jacob. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes for digesting lactose.

tossups.p: This system’s three structural genes are copied together into a single messenger RNA that carries the instructions for three different proteins, a kind of message called polycistronic [“pol-ee-sis-TROH-nik”]. One promoter controls all three of those genes, so they switch on and off together.
tossups.r: Lactose switches them on. For 10 points, name this classic example of gene regulation in E. coli.

tossups.p: Charles Yanofsky [“yuh-NOFF-skee”] studied a contrasting set of E. coli genes that is switched off when tryptophan is plentiful. Unlike that “repressible” set, this set of genes is “inducible,” staying off until its food molecule appears.
tossups.r: That food molecule is lactose. For 10 points, name this set of genes explained by Jacob and Monod.

tossups.p: The two scientists who explained this system shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with their Pasteur Institute colleague André Lwoff, who had studied viruses that hide inside bacteria. Their 1961 model of this system also predicted a short-lived “messenger” molecule that carries genetic instructions to ribosomes.
tossups.r: That molecule is messenger RNA. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes that is switched on by lactose.

tossups.p: Glucose keeps this system quiet partly through “inducer exclusion,” in which taking in glucose blocks the permease that would carry another sugar into the cell. Glucose also lowers cyclic AMP, so the activator protein CAP cannot help switch this system on.
tossups.r: This system’s inducer comes from lactose. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes studied by Jacob and Monod.

tossups.p: One gene in this system makes a permease, a membrane protein that pulls a sugar into the cell along with a hydrogen ion. Biotech companies often use parts of this system to switch on genes for medicines made in bacteria.
tossups.r: Normally, its repressor sits on the operator. For 10 points, name this set of E. coli genes that is switched on by lactose.

tossups.p: This system’s repressor is made by a gene labeled I, which sits just before the system’s promoter. An E. coli cell holds very few copies of that repressor, yet they keep the other genes almost completely off until the right sugar arrives.
tossups.r: That sugar is lactose. For 10 points, name this set of genes explained by Jacob and Monod.

Monod wrote _Chance and Necessity_ (1970) and Jacob wrote _The Logic of Life_; both fought Nazi Germany in World War II
Jacob and Monod’s 1961 model predicted a short-lived messenger molecule: messenger RNA
Charles Yanofsky studied the contrasting trp genes, which are switched off when tryptophan is plentiful

trap.title: Lac, not trp
trap.body: Bacteria have more than one famous operon. The trp operon makes the amino acid tryptophan and is repressible: it is normally on and gets switched off when tryptophan piles up. The lac operon is inducible: it is normally off and gets switched on when lactose shows up. Players also mix up the lac operon with lactase, the enzyme people use to digest milk sugar.
trap.fix: Lactose, allolactose, beta-galactosidase, IPTG, X-gal, CAP, or Jacob and Monod mean the lac operon; tryptophan, attenuation, and Charles Yanofsky mean the trp operon. Saying just “operon” earns a prompt, so be ready to add “lac.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Lac operon (accept lactose operon; prompt on operon; do not accept “trp operon”)
